tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

schema.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
schema.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

content.content:
## Features - **Display settings:** choose System, Light or Dark, text size from 100% to 150%, and standard or accessible blue/orange gain and loss colors. Changes apply immediately and are saved. ### Tray and hotkey - **Tray icon:** the company logo with an up/down badge. Hover for the quote, left-click to open the window, or to close it again the way the hotkey does if it's already open and focused. Right-click holds every on/off setting: show pre-market/after-hours, show change as % or $, always on top, unload window when minimized, start hidden, launch at login, check for updates automatically and, on macOS, show price in menu bar. If something needs attention (the hotkey is taken, or launch at login could not be changed), the tooltip ends with a ⚠ line. - **Global hotkey** (default `Ctrl+Alt+K` on Windows, `⌘⇧K` on macOS): opens the window, or minimizes it if it's focused. On macOS, where tickr has no Dock icon, it hides the window instead (or unloads it, when unload is on). Change it in [Settings](#settings-and-keybinds). If another app owns the hotkey at startup, the window footer shows the error until you pick one that works. - **Launch at login** is off until you turn it on. Once on, it survives upgrades: tickr re-registers itself if an installer removed the entry, unless you turned it off in Task Manager. - **Unload when minimized** (on by default): minimizing destroys the web view, so the app drops to one process using about 7 MB. The hotkey reopens it already painted with the last chart and quote, then refreshes in the background. The window opens on a dark or light background to match the OS theme, so it never flashes white. Windows may hide new tray icons in the overflow menu (^). Drag it onto the taskbar to keep it visible. ### Chart - **Symbol and range:** search to change the symbol, pick a range from 1D to Max and switch between line and candles. Search filters by asset type and exchange, and exact ticker matches come first. Press Enter on a typed ticker to open it directly. 1D, 5D and 1M charts reload about once a minute. - **Sessions and time zone:** extended-hours candles can be shown or hidden on the chart without changing the tray quote setting. Pre- and post-market sessions are shaded, and chart times can use the exchange or local time zone. - **Second chart:** the toggle (J by default) opens a second chart pane, side by side or stacked, with its own symbol and range. Crosshair time is linked across both charts. Turn on **Sync** to pan and zoom both panes together. tickr saves the layout across launches. - **Recent symbols and history:** focus the empty search box to see the last 10 symbols you viewed. The Back and Forward buttons (or Alt+Left and Alt+Right) step through this session's symbols, and B jumps to the previous one, so pressing it again toggles between two. - **Price scales:** linear, logarithmic, or percentage change rebased to the first visible candle as you pan and zoom. Press L to cycle scales. - **Drawings:** the toolbar places levels, trendlines, text and freehand pen strokes, saved per symbol. Keys 1 to 5 pick the level, trendline, text, ruler and pen tools. ## Screenshots The demo and screenshots use sample data. Click an image to view it at full size. | | | | :---: | :---: | | [![Five-year and one-year AAPL charts with linked crosshairs](assets/screenshots/split-charts.png)](assets/screenshots/split-charts.png)
**Linked charts** let you inspect the same date in two date ranges. | [![Historical AAPL chart with bar replay controls](assets/screenshots/bar-replay.png)](assets/screenshots/bar-replay.png)
**Bar replay** reveals candles at your pace. | | [![Replay chart with a buy fill and the simulated position panel](assets/screenshots/paper-trading.png)](assets/screenshots/paper-trading.png)
**Paper trading** shows the filled order and open position. | [![Historical practice result with return, bars held and a Skip comparison](assets/screenshots/historical-practice.png)](assets/screenshots/historical-practice.png)
**Historical practice** shows how a trade performed against skipping. | | [![AAPL candle chart with an OHLC tooltip and event markers](assets/screenshots/chart.png)](assets/screenshots/chart.png)
**Chart** shows candle details and lets you copy a PNG or CSV. | [![AAPL chart with indicator overlays, RSI and a technical analysis score](assets/screenshots/technicals.webp)](assets/screenshots/technicals.webp)
**Technicals** computes signals and targets from the chart's candles. | | [![Market overview with indices, macro quotes, sectors and movers](assets/screenshots/market.png)](assets/screenshots/market.png)
**Market** groups indices, sectors and daily movers. | [![Stock watchlist with session prices and named groups](assets/screenshots/watchlist.png)](assets/screenshots/watchlist.png)
**Watchlist** keeps prices and session moves for starred symbols together. | ## Data Quotes, charts, news and fundamentals come from Yahoo Finance's public chart, search and quoteSummary endpoints. They are not an official API and can change or rate-limit without notice, and quotes may be delayed. Logos come from [Elbstream](https://elbstream.com/logos)'s logo API (formerly Parqet); the **Logos by Elbstream** link in the footer is the attribution its free tier requires. Analysis and sentiment run on your machine. Not investment advice. ## Files | What | Windows | macOS | | --- | --- | --- | | Settings | `%APPDATA%\tickr\settings.json` | `~/Library/Application Support/tickr/` | | AI credentials | `%APPDATA%\tickr\.env.local` | `~/Library/Application Support/tickr/` | | Logo, AI tone and event analysis cache | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\tickr\` | `~/Library/Caches/tickr/` | | Logs | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\dev.tickr.desktop\logs\tickr.log` | `~/Library/Logs/dev.tickr.desktop/` | Logs rotate at 1 MB and keep two old files. Attach `tickr.log` to bug reports. Uninstalling on Windows removes the launch-at-login entry. Check "Delete the application data" in the uninstaller to also remove settings, the logo cache, logs and WebView data. ## Development ### Build Requirements: Rust 1.85+, Node 20+, and the [Tauri 2 prerequisites](https://tauri.app/start/prerequisites/). ```bash npm install npm run tauri dev # dev build with hot reload npx tauri build # installer (NSIS on Windows, .app and .dmg on macOS) ``` `npx tauri build` also signs the updater bundles, which needs the private key (see [Updater key](#updater-key)). Without it, skip the updater artifacts: ### Tests ```bash cd src-tauri && cargo test # technical analysis (indicators, patterns, Fibonacci, scoring), quote, analyst, earnings, rating change, stats, financials, market and news parsing, headline sentiment, sessions, tray tooltip and title, icon compositing, settings, watchlist symbols and groups, economic calendar and watchlist dates, update menu labels cd src-tauri && cargo test -- --ignored live # analyst, market, financials, economic calendar and watchlist date fetches against Yahoo (network) npm test # formatters, watchlist sort, calendar filters and dates, hotkey recording and display, keybinds npm run check # svelte-check ``` ### Layout ``` src-tauri/src/ quote.rs Yahoo chart/search: fetch, parse, market session, extended-hours price analysis/ local technical analysis: indicators (RSI, SMA/EMA, ATR, σ), patterns, Fibonacci swing, score and targets analyst.rs Yahoo quoteSummary: cookie/crumb session, consensus and price targets, 12 h cache earnings.rs Yahoo quoteSummary: past EPS reports and next report date events.rs Yahoo economic calendar: any week, all countries, paged; AI analysis of one event on demand, 6 h cache calendar.rs Yahoo quoteSummary calendarEvents: earnings and ex-dividend dates per watchlist symbol, 6 h cache grades.rs Yahoo quoteSummary: analyst upgrades, downgrades and initiations stats.rs Yahoo quoteSummary: key statistics in labeled sections financials.rs Yahoo fundamentals-timeseries: annual and quarterly revenue, net income, gross and operating profit, free cash flow, 12 h cache market.rs Yahoo batch quotes and screeners: indices, macro, sectors, top movers news.rs Yahoo search news: 20 latest headlines, newest first, web links only sentiment.rs headline tone (positive, negative, neutral) from a financial keyword list poller.rs Balanced/Low-power refresh, alert cadence, system wake and network recovery tray.rs tooltip text, macOS menu bar title, and the right-click menu trayicon.rs icon (32 px, 36 px on macOS): logo in a rounded square plus a direction badge logo.rs Elbstream logo fetch with a disk cache window.rs create, OS theme background, reveal after first paint, unload on minimize, geometry hotkey.rs global shortcut register/swap with rollback commands.rs window commands and the injected first-frame payload settings.rs JSON settings in the OS config dir autostart.rs launch at login: restores the Run entry after upgrades updater.rs background update checks, tray menu state, install and restart src-tauri/windows/hooks.nsh NSIS uninstall hook: autostart entry and app data .github/workflows/ ci.yml (checks on push/PR), release.yml (installers, updater bundles and latest.json on tag push) ui/src/ App, Left (ticker and details), Chart (canvas, analysis overlays), Technicals, Analysts, Earnings, Stats, Market, Events, WatchCalendar, News, Watchlist, Search, Settings, Footer ``` ### Memory (Windows 11, release build) | State | Processes | Private | | --- | --- | --- | | Window open | 7 | 132 MB | | Window unloaded (tray only) | 1 | 7 MB | ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Bug reports should include `tickr.log`, your OS and the tickr version. ## Market data Yahoo is the default; no provider configuration is required. To use Alpaca, open Settings > Market data, choose Alpaca, select a feed, enter your key ID and secret, then Save and Test connection. Blank key fields keep saved credentials. Clear keys removes them and switches back to Yahoo. Free Alpaca keys provide real-time IEX trades for US stocks. IEX covers one exchange; the paid SIP feed provides consolidated US market data and requires the appropriate subscription. Only symbols of one to five uppercase letters use Alpaca. Indices, crypto, foreign listings and symbols such as BRK-B continue to use Yahoo. Yahoo also supplies company metadata, sessions, corporate actions and quote volume. Alpaca supplies selected-stock prices and chart candles, with automatic Yahoo fallback on failure. The footer shows the actual quote source and stream status. Watchlist quotes and alerts still use Yahoo because free Alpaca keys allow 200 requests per minute. The stream subscribes only to the selected stock, using one connection (the free plan allows one connection and 30 symbols). Polling continues as a backstop. Authentication, connection-limit and subscription errors pause stream retries until the symbol or provider configuration changes. Keys are stored in `.env.local` in tickr's OS configuration directory, alongside the AI configuration, and are never returned to the page. `settings.json` stores only the provider and feed. Changing market data settings reloads the chart. ## License MIT. Company logos are provided by [Elbstream](https://elbstream.com/logos). ====== ===CUR ====== cat: README.md: invalid utf-8 sequence of 1 bytes from index 0 ====== .claude/launch.json .gitignore Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\Joe\.claude\skills\codex-delegate

# codex-delegate

Offload bounded work to Codex. Claude stays orchestrator and reviewer.

## When to delegate

Delegate when ALL hold:
- Spec fits in one self-contained prompt (no need for this chat's history).
- Touches roughly 1-5 files.
- Verifiable by a command (tests, build, lint) or by reading the diff.
- Not security-sensitive, not architecture, not a subtle/concurrency bug.

Good fits: test suites, boilerplate, docs/README, mechanical refactors, small features with clear spec, second-opinion review, codebase Q&A.
Keep in Claude: design decisions, ambiguous requirements, cross-repo changes, debugging that needs iteration.

## Gate (automatic)

`codex-run.ps1` runs `codex-gate.ps1` first. It blocks (exit 3, `GATE_BLOCKED: <why>`) unless the Codex login is on the **plus** plan and neither the 5h nor weekly window is >= 95% used (read from the newest `~/.codex/sessions` rate_limits entry; a window past its reset counts as 0%). On block: do the task yourself or with a normal subagent. Do not retry in a loop. Check without running: `& "<skill dir>\codex-gate.ps1"`.

## Model choice (Claude decides, always medium effort)

- `gpt-6.1-sol` (default): routine work: tests, boilerplate, docs, mechanical refactors, small clear features, reviews.
- `gpt-6-astra`: harder medium work: several interacting files, some ambiguity, tricky logic. Costs more usage; if the task needs more than this, keep it in Claude.

Pass with `-Model gpt-6-astra`.

## How

Run the wrapper (PowerShell). The scripts sit next to this SKILL.md; use this skill's base directory as `<skill dir>`:

```powershell
& "<skill dir>\codex-run.ps1" -Prompt "<task>" -Cwd "<project dir>" [-Write] [-Model gpt-6.1-sol|gpt-6-astra] [-TimeoutSec 600]
```

- Default is read-only sandbox (review, research, analysis).
- `-Write` = `workspace-write` sandbox: Codex may edit files inside `-Cwd` only.
- Long jobs: run with `run_in_background` and wait for the notification.
- Output = Codex's final message. On failure prints `CODEX_FAILED` / `CODEX_TIMEOUT` plus stderr tail.

## Prompt template

Codex has no access to this conversation. Include:
1. Goal (one sentence).
2. Exact files/dirs in scope, and what NOT to touch.
3. Conventions to follow (point at an example file).
4. Done criteria + verify command (e.g. `npm test`).
5. "Do not commit. Report changed files and anything unverified."

## After Codex returns (mandatory)

1. `git diff` / `git status` in the project. Read the diff.
2. Re-run the verify command yourself. Do not trust Codex's "tests pass."
3. Fix small issues directly; for big misses, re-delegate with sharper prompt or take over.
4. Tell the user what Codex did and what you verified.

## Rules

- Never delegate with secrets in the prompt.
- Never pass `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`; wrapper never uses it.
- Codex edits are uncommitted; Claude owns commits.
- One Codex job per file set at a time; no parallel writers on same files.
- If `codex.exe` missing: `~/.codex/.sandbox-bin/codex.exe` ships with the Codex desktop app; reinstall the app.

1	# BioHacks McMaster 2026: Haptic Core Stability Backpack
2	
3	A wearable backpack for Alex Chen (47, ALS) that counteracts his gait and balance problems so he can keep teaching: it senses trunk tilt and sway, taps his torso and speaks cues through a phone app when fatigue or foot-drop sway is detected, and streams data to a clinician dashboard with AI-generated reports. A tabletop gyroscope rig demonstrates the active-correction version. See `PATIENT_CASE.md` for the patient case (Alex Chen, ALS) and design implications, and `plan/` for the working plan. Links are at the bottom of this file.
4	
5	## Event facts
6	
7	- Event: BioHacks 2026 by BioEng4Youth, McMaster University, Hamilton. Official MLH Member Event.
8	- Format: every team solves one patient-centred neurological case, revealed at the opening ceremony. Pitches should be clear and evidence-backed. Judges come from sponsors and partners.
9	- Sat Nov 7: opening 10:00 AM, team formation 11:00 AM, team registration and track lock-in closes 12:00 PM.
10	- Sun Nov 8: submissions due 11:30 AM, expo judging 1:30 to 3:00 PM (judges visit tables), closing and winners 4:30 PM.
11	- Work must be made during the event. Software, hardware, 3D prints and design concepts are all accepted.
12	- Devpost submission needs: problem description, how it works, what was built, links to code/CAD/slides, a short video demo, every teammate added, and a track selection matching the team form.
13	- Devpost: https://devpost.com/submit-to/30296-biohacks-2026/manage/submissions
14	
15	## Tracks and prizes
16	
17	Each team competes in exactly one track. Sponsor prizes are opted into at submission. Wearables rubric (out of 100): clinical grounding 20, design and function 30 (prototype or demo counts), usability in daily life 20, feasibility 15, communication 15. $1,000 goes to the top team overall.
18	
19	- Main track: Wearable Devices and Quality of Life: help Alex keep one thing that matters to him as his abilities change. 2 cash winners.
20	- Best Use of Gemini API: examples given are chatbots and research summarizers.
21	- Best Use of ElevenLabs: must integrate ElevenLabs audio.
22	- Best Use of Tiger Data: judged on innovative, impactful and performance-driven use.
23	- Best Use of Vultr: judged on pushing the limits of cloud or GPU-based builds.
24	- Best Domain Name from GoDaddy Registry: must register a domain with GoDaddy Registry.
25	- Best 3D Print by Bambu Lab: best 3D-printed design.
26	
27	## Locked decisions
28	
29	- Pitch goal: staying in a classroom in June 2027. Target moments: walking around the room and standing at the board, with late-day fatigue in mind.
30	- Mechanism is hybrid. (1) Working wearable: cues timed to the gait cycle plus spoken cues when fatigue or foot-drop sway is detected. (2) Tabletop gyroscope rig: a spinning flywheel on a servo gimbal that physically resists a tipping dummy torso, showing the active-correction version, based on TU Delft's GyBAR (see `PATIENT_CASE.md`).
31	- Form factor stays a backpack: as light as possible, no chest pressure, closures usable without fine finger control.
32	- Haptics are servo tappers, not vibration motors. The MLH hardware lab has no vibration motors or haptic drivers. Servo split: 2 Grove Servos as left/right tappers, 1 as the rig's gimbal, 1 spare. The Grove Buzzer is a piezo and cannot vibrate against the body.
33	- Gyro rig flywheel: hobby DC motor through the Grove Motor/Servo Driver Board (no ESC needed). Weaker than brushless, so use a heavy metal disk and tune the demo for a visible effect.
34	- No moving weights. Shifting a small mass barely moves the center of mass, adds mechanical risk, and could destabilize the wearer.
35	- Raspberry Pi 4B is the brain. The lab Arduino model is unknown and a plain Uno has no wireless. The Pi has WiFi and BLE built in, reads the Grove 3-axis accelerometer over I2C, drives the servos (directly or via the Grove Motor/Servo Driver Board), and runs from a USB-C power bank.
36	- The accelerometer has no gyro, so tilt comes from the low-pass filtered gravity vector. Expect noise while walking; tune filtering and thresholds early.
37	- Data path: Pi POSTs readings and events to Next.js over WiFi. Next.js runs with a custom server and a `ws` WebSocket server on a Vultr VM, writes to Tiger Data, and pushes events to the phone app. Vercel was rejected because its serverless functions do not hold persistent WebSockets.
38	- Phone app: Expo (React Native) on iOS, running in Expo Go. It connects to the backend WebSocket and plays ElevenLabs spoken cues (for example, slow down or lift the right foot). Never clone Alex's voice; voice banking is one of his stated reluctances. BLE was dropped because BLE libraries need a custom dev build (Xcode or EAS plus Apple signing), and the Pi has WiFi anyway.
39	- Gemini clinician reports: generated automatically after each session and on demand from the dashboard over a chosen time range. Gemini summarizes and reasons over stored data; it does not train the tilt model.
40	- Tiger Data (TimescaleDB): all four ideas, with focus on (1) high-frequency IMU ingestion into a hypertable with continuous aggregates per minute/hour/day and (3) anomaly-window queries that flag unusual sway and feed Gemini. Also (2) long-term progress tracking with compression and (4) a multi-patient clinician view.
41	- Vultr: level 1 is the VM hosting the real-time pipeline, with live tilt-to-voice latency shown on the dashboard. Stretch: train a small sway classifier on a Vultr GPU instance from labeled data (stable, swaying, near-fall) and serve it from the VM.
42	- Bambu Lab prints: ergonomic Pi/electronics enclosure against the spine, clip-on servo tapper pods for adjustable placement, a rigid accelerometer mount at the lower back, and the gyro rig's flywheel housing and gimbal frame. Ask an organizer to print.
43	- Team: 4 people, one owner per area.
44	
45	## MLH hardware lab (relevant parts)
46	
47	Raspberry Pi 4B kits (9), Arduinos of unspecified model with Base Shields (12), Grove 3 Axis Digital Accelerometer (10), Grove Servo (4), Grove Motor/Servo Driver Board (5), Grove Buzzer (10), JBL Go 3 (2), Grove cables, jumpers, breadboards, resistors, capacitors, multimeter. No ESP32, gyro, vibration motors, haptic drivers or batteries are listed. Full list: https://guide.mlh.com/organizer-resources/hardware-lab-contents
48	
49	## Open questions
50	
51	- Exact Arduino model. If it is an UNO R4 WiFi, Nano 33 BLE or Nano ESP32 it has wireless. Either way it could run the gyro rig on its own (accelerometer, DC flywheel motor, gimbal servo) so the rig is independent of the wearable.
52	- Source of the hobby DC motor for the flywheel. The lab lists brushless, stepper and servo motors but no plain DC motor.
53	- Domain name for GoDaddy Registry is not chosen.
54	- Owner assignment for the 4 areas (hardware/firmware, backend/data, app/audio, dashboard/CAD) is not set.
55	- Servo count: the lab lists 4 Grove Servos total and we need 3. Reserve them at the hardware table.
56	
57	## Working rules
58	
59	- Do not commit or push unless explicitly told to.
60	- Never use em dashes in code or text.
61	- Expo judging is in MCCD 7110 and 7120. Ask an organizer to 3D print parts.
62	- Ask for clarification and design decisions before starting tasks whenever anything is ambiguous; do not assume.
63	- Write paragraphs as continuous lines without mid-paragraph line breaks.
64	- Only comment complex edge cases; keep comments concise.
65	- Use concise, idiomatic names.
66	- No redundant null checks or boilerplate error catching where normal propagation is fine.
67	
68	## Links
69	- hardware components: https://guide.mlh.com/organizer-resources/hardware-lab-contents
70	- main link: https://www.bioeng4youth.ca/
71	- devpost: https://devpost.com/submit-to/30296-biohacks-2026/manage/submissions

9	- Two-storey house. Bedroom and the only full bathroom are upstairs, 14 stairs.
10

12	
13	- Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), limb onset, with early bulbar and respiratory involvement. Diagnosed 14 July 2026 after about 27 months of symptoms.
14	- June 2024: whiteboard handwriting faded; right thumb and index finger fatigued quickly. Carpal tunnel release (Jan 2025) did not help despite normal wrist studies.
15	- Spring 2025: right foot drop, progressing despite physiotherapy. Then falls, a cane, and spreading weakness.
16	- Tests: EMG shows widespread active denervation in four regions with normal sensory conduction. CK mildly raised (470 U/L). Neurofilament light chain 88 pg/mL (reference below 15). Genetic panel negative (C9orf72, SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and 28 others). MRI shows corticospinal tract changes and a motor band sign.
17	- Prognosis as communicated: median survival two to four years from onset, wide range. Feeding tube, night ventilation and communication decisions are better made early.
18	
19	## Current status (September 2026)
20	
21	- ALSFRS-R 32/48, declining about 0.6 points per month.
22	- Grip: right 3/5 with pinch lasting only seconds; left 4/5 and weakening. Uses a spoon in the left hand. Handwriting illegible after about ten minutes. Needs help with buttons, zips and shoelaces in the morning.
23	- Speech intelligible but effortful by late afternoon. Reading rate drops from 165 wpm at 9 AM to 118 wpm at 4 PM; sentence intelligibility from 98% to 91%.
24	- Swallowing: coughs on thin liquids; solids and thickened liquids fine. Meals take 35 to 40 minutes. Weight down from 86 kg to 77.5 kg. Calorie supplement started.
25	- Breathing: FVC 76% sitting, 61% supine. Sleeps on two pillows.
26	- Cognition: reduced verbal fluency and executive function; memory, language and visuospatial scores normal.
27	- Mobility: two falls in three months, both after 6 PM, on the stairs or at dusk. 10 m walk in 14.2 s with a cane. Wears a right ankle-foot orthosis at school but not at home.
28	- Medications: riluzole 50 mg twice daily since July 2026 (tolerated). Edaravone declined for now.

33	- Drives an automatic with his left foot; has not told his insurer.
34	- Alone at home on non-teaching days and from the end of school until 4:30 PM.
35	- Has declined a stairlift "for now". Stopped eating in the staff room and stopped the end-of-day recap.

39	- Stay in a classroom in June 2027.
40	- Keep cooking Sunday family meals, even if it takes all afternoon.
41	- Be "reachable and useful" while alone in the afternoons.
42	- Attend his daughter's graduation in two years without a wheelchair.

48	- Stairlift.
49	- Asking for classroom accommodations.

53	Dr. Priya Raman (family physician), Dr. Marcus Oyelaran (plastic and hand surgery), Daniela Ferreira (physiotherapist), Dr. Hannah Weiss-Okafor (neurologist), Dr. Thanh Nguyen (neuroradiology), a regional ALS clinic every three months, plus speech-language pathology, dietitian, occupational therapy, respiratory, social work and ALS Canada.
54

57	Design a device or tool that helps Alex keep one thing that matters to him as his abilities change. The organizers highlight his afternoon weakness, needing to be heard in class, being alone until 4:30 PM, his falls on the stairs, and the risk that assistive devices go unused when nobody asks the user what they want. The MLH hardware lab is open all weekend.

60	
61	- Clinical grounding: 20
62	- Design and function: 30, including whether a prototype or demonstration supports it
63	- Usability in daily life: 20, including comfort, adapting as the condition progresses, and day-to-day use
64	- Feasibility: 15
65	- Communication: 15
66

68

70	
71	- Goal we center on: staying in a classroom in June 2027. Target moments are walking around the room (between desks and the board) and standing at the board, both of which get harder as weakness and fatigue build through the afternoon.
72	- Intent: counteract the gait and balance problem rather than cure it, so Alex can keep walking and standing while teaching with a much lower fall risk.
73	- His falls come from motor weakness (right foot drop, fatigue) with normal sensory conduction, not a sensory or vestibular deficit. Tactile cues alone are weakly grounded for ALS, which is why the concept pairs cues with active correction.
74	- Active correction precedent: TU Delft's GyBAR, a backpack-like control moment gyroscope that applies corrective moments to the trunk (Lemus et al., Scientific Reports 2020, DOI 10.1038/s41598-020-66760-w). Tested on healthy and chronic stroke participants, not ALS, so present it as a promising direction, not proven for Alex.
75	- Risk is time-dependent: weakness and speech worsen through the afternoon, and both falls were after 6 PM, on stairs or at dusk. Time-of-day trends belong in the data and the reports.
76	- Form factor stays a backpack. Keep it as light as possible and put no pressure on the chest, given his weight loss (86 to 77.5 kg) and reduced FVC (76% sitting, 61% supine). Closures and controls must not need fine finger control (no small buttons, zips or clasps).
77	- He resists visible assistive devices and classroom accommodations. The device should look like a normal backpack and stay discreet in front of students, and the pitch should show we designed around what he wants.
78	- The ALS clinic sees him every three months. Continuous between-visit data (sway, gait changes, time-of-day patterns) summarized for the physio and neurologist is the clinical value of the Gemini reports.
79	- ElevenLabs is for spoken cues only. Voice banking is a stated reluctance, so never clone his voice or frame the audio as voice banking.
80	- Relevant dataset: Gait in Neurodegenerative Disease (PhysioNet), foot-force and stride data including ALS, open download. Could inform thresholds or the stretch sway classifier.

# Patient Case: Alex Chen (ALS)

Source: https://www.bioeng4youth.ca/BioHacks-2026-Hacker-Package.pdf (fictional case provided by BioHacks 2026). This is a working summary for design decisions; check the PDF for exact wording before quoting it in the pitch.

## Who he is

- 47, male, right-handed. Senior biology teacher at a Hamilton high school for 19 years. Former cross-country coach and half-marathon runner; stopped running in spring 2025.
- Lives in Westdale with partner Jordan (medical radiation technologist, 7 AM to 4 PM shifts) and children Maya (16) and Leo (14).
- Two-storey house. Bedroom and the only full bathroom are upstairs, 14 stairs.

## Diagnosis and course

- Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), limb onset, with early bulbar and respiratory involvement. Diagnosed 14 July 2026 after about 27 months of symptoms.
- June 2024: whiteboard handwriting faded; right thumb and index finger fatigued quickly. Carpal tunnel release (Jan 2025) did not help despite normal wrist studies.
- Spring 2025: right foot drop, progressing despite physiotherapy. Then falls, a cane, and spreading weakness.
- Tests: EMG shows widespread active denervation in four regions with normal sensory conduction. CK mildly raised (470 U/L). Neurofilament light chain 88 pg/mL (reference below 15). Genetic panel negative (C9orf72, SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and 28 others). MRI shows corticospinal tract changes and a motor band sign.
- Prognosis as communicated: median survival two to four years from onset, wide range. Feeding tube, night ventilation and communication decisions are better made early.

## Current status (September 2026)

- ALSFRS-R 32/48, declining about 0.6 points per month.
- Grip: right 3/5 with pinch lasting only seconds; left 4/5 and weakening. Uses a spoon in the left hand. Handwriting illegible after about ten minutes. Needs help with buttons, zips and shoelaces in the morning.
- Speech intelligible but effortful by late afternoon. Reading rate drops from 165 wpm at 9 AM to 118 wpm at 4 PM; sentence intelligibility from 98% to 91%.
- Swallowing: coughs on thin liquids; solids and thickened liquids fine. Meals take 35 to 40 minutes. Weight down from 86 kg to 77.5 kg. Calorie supplement started.
- Breathing: FVC 76% sitting, 61% supine. Sleeps on two pillows.
- Cognition: reduced verbal fluency and executive function; memory, language and visuospatial scores normal.
- Mobility: two falls in three months, both after 6 PM, on the stairs or at dusk. 10 m walk in 14.2 s with a cane. Wears a right ankle-foot orthosis at school but not at home.
- Medications: riluzole 50 mg twice daily since July 2026 (tolerated). Edaravone declined for now.

## Daily life

- Still teaches four classes a day. Has not taken up the stool or microphone the school offered.
- Drives an automatic with his left foot; has not told his insurer.
- Alone at home on non-teaching days and from the end of school until 4:30 PM.
- Has declined a stairlift "for now". Stopped eating in the staff room and stopped the end-of-day recap.

## Goals

- Stay in a classroom in June 2027.
- Keep cooking Sunday family meals, even if it takes all afternoon.
- Be "reachable and useful" while alone in the afternoons.
- Attend his daughter's graduation in two years without a wheelchair.
- Be remembered by his children as their dad, not as a patient.

## Reluctances

- Voice banking ("it feels like giving up").
- Stairlift.
- Asking for classroom accommodations.

## Care team

Dr. Priya Raman (family physician), Dr. Marcus Oyelaran (plastic and hand surgery), Daniela Ferreira (physiotherapist), Dr. Hannah Weiss-Okafor (neurologist), Dr. Thanh Nguyen (neuroradiology), a regional ALS clinic every three months, plus speech-language pathology, dietitian, occupational therapy, respiratory, social work and ALS Canada.

## Wearables track prompt

Design a device or tool that helps Alex keep one thing that matters to him as his abilities change. The organizers highlight his afternoon weakness, needing to be heard in class, being alone until 4:30 PM, his falls on the stairs, and the risk that assistive devices go unused when nobody asks the user what they want. The MLH hardware lab is open all weekend.

## Wearables rubric (out of 100)

- Clinical grounding: 20
- Design and function: 30, including whether a prototype or demonstration supports it
- Usability in daily life: 20, including comfort, adapting as the condition progresses, and day-to-day use
- Feasibility: 15
- Communication: 15

Each criterion has four levels. Judges score each project and name their top three; combined rankings pick two winners per track. There is also $1,000 for the top team overall.

## Design implications for our project

- Goal we center on: staying in a classroom in June 2027. Target moments are walking around the room (between desks and the board) and standing at the board, both of which get harder as weakness and fatigue build through the afternoon.
- Intent: counteract the gait and balance problem rather than cure it, so Alex can keep walking and standing while teaching with a much lower fall risk.
- His falls come from motor weakness (right foot drop, fatigue) with normal sensory conduction, not a sensory or vestibular deficit. Tactile cues alone are weakly grounded for ALS, which is why the concept pairs cues with active correction.
- Active correction precedent: TU Delft's GyBAR, a backpack-like control moment gyroscope that applies corrective moments to the trunk (Lemus et al., Scientific Reports 2020, DOI 10.1038/s41598-020-66760-w). Tested on healthy and chronic stroke participants, not ALS, so present it as a promising direction, not proven for Alex.
- Risk is time-dependent: weakness and speech worsen through the afternoon, and both falls were after 6 PM, on stairs or at dusk. Time-of-day trends belong in the data and the reports.
- Form factor stays a backpack. Keep it as light as possible and put no pressure on the chest, given his weight loss (86 to 77.5 kg) and reduced FVC (76% sitting, 61% supine). Closures and controls must not need fine finger control (no small buttons, zips or clasps).
- He resists visible assistive devices and classroom accommodations. The device should look like a normal backpack and stay discreet in front of students, and the pitch should show we designed around what he wants.
- The ALS clinic sees him every three months. Continuous between-visit data (sway, gait changes, time-of-day patterns) summarized for the physio and neurologist is the clinical value of the Gemini reports.
- ElevenLabs is for spoken cues only. Voice banking is a stated reluctance, so never clone his voice or frame the audio as voice banking.
- Relevant dataset: Gait in Neurodegenerative Disease (PhysioNet), foot-force and stride data including ALS, open download. Could inform thresholds or the stretch sway classifier.

1:# Adaptive AFO Care Dashboard and Backend: Design
3:Date: 2026-11-07. Project: BioHacks McMaster 2026, patient Alex Chen (47, ALS). See `docs/plan/PATIENT_CASE.md`. This replaces the earlier backpack-focused dashboard design.
7:[Omitted long matching line]
12:- Ingest AFO data from the Raspberry Pi into Tiger Data (TimescaleDB).
13:- Show stability metrics: ankle angle, toe clearance, gait events and cadence, stair ascent and descent, assist level, a composite stability score.
15:- Progression insights: stability score trend, foot drop severity trend (dorsiflexion, clearance, assist needed over months), clinic scores (ALSFRS-R, 10 m walk) entered manually and plotted next to sensor data.
17:- An AFO simulator posing as the Pi, plus seeded history, so everything demos without hardware.
26:- Pi firmware and AFO mechanics (they only need the API contract).
33:- Overstating evidence: adaptive AFO assist is a prototype, not a proven ALS treatment.
37:- Device: adaptive AFO for foot drop, focused on preventing stair falls. Data comes from a Raspberry Pi.
39:- Sensors shown: ankle angle, toe clearance, gait events and stairs, assist level.
40:- Adaptation: assist rises automatically with fatigue (when clearance drops).
60:- `web/scripts/simulate.ts`: AFO simulator posting like the Pi. `web/scripts/seed.ts`: 90 days of history plus clinic visits.
69:type EventType = 'near_trip' | 'fall' | 'assist_increase' | 'assist_decrease' | 'stairs_start' | 'stairs_end' | 'afo_on' | 'afo_off';
73:  time: string;           // toe-off
75:  minClearanceMm: number; // toe clearance in swing
84:  avgClearanceMm: number; avgPeakDorsiDeg: number; avgAssistPct: number;
87:interface HourCell { day: string; hour: number; avgClearanceMm: number; nearTrips: number }
101:Stability score (0 to 100, my call, tunable in `lib/metrics.ts`): weighted from clearance vs 2 cm target, peak dorsiflexion vs baseline, stride time variability, near-trips per 100 stair steps, and assist needed. Higher is steadier.
106:- `steps(time, patient_id, terrain, min_clearance_mm, peak_dorsi_deg, stride_ms, assist_pct)`: hypertable, compression after 7 days.
110:- Continuous aggregates on `steps`: `steps_1h` and `steps_1d` (counts by terrain, avg clearance, avg dorsiflexion, avg assist, stride variability).
111:- Anomaly query: hours whose avg clearance falls below the 30-day mean minus 2 standard deviations, plus all stair near-trips. Feeds Gemini.
129:- Physician report (on demand over a chosen range): Stability findings, Progression vs baseline (foot drop severity, assist trend, clinic scores), Suggested physiotherapy focus (for example ankle dorsiflexor work, stair strategy, fatigue pacing, AFO assist tuning), Questions for the next visit.
130:- System prompt forbids diagnosis, frames recs as suggestions for the treating physiotherapist, notes the AFO is a prototype. UI shows "AI-generated summary, not medical advice" under every report.
134:- `scripts/simulate.ts`: posts to `/api/ingest` like the Pi. 100 Hz ankle samples shaped like a gait cycle, a step every ~1.1 s, periodic stair bouts, clearance falling through the afternoon and evening with assist rising to compensate, rare near-trips on stairs. Key `n` forces a stair near-trip, `s` toggles a stair bout.
135:- `scripts/seed.ts`: 90 days of steps and events with slow decline (clearance and dorsiflexion down, assist up, stability score drifting down), worse afternoons and after 6 PM, plus clinic visits about every 3 months with ALSFRS-R and 10 m walk values consistent with the patient case (10 m walk 14.2 s at the latest visit).
151:- Live: ankle angle trace (last 10 s), last-step clearance vs 2 cm target, current assist %, terrain badge (Level / Stairs up / Stairs down), wearing status.
152:- Stability metrics: KPI row (stability score, avg clearance, peak dorsiflexion, assist %, stair near-trips per 100 stair steps) with deltas vs previous period; range picker (7, 30, 90 days).
153:- Progression: 90-day lines for stability score, clearance, dorsiflexion and assist, with clinic visit markers; clinic scores table with an "Add visit" form (ALSFRS-R, 10 m walk, note).
154:- Time of day: hour-by-day clearance heatmap (14 days) with near-trip dots.
